title: Logarithmic Interface Scaling — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Logarithmic Interface Scaling's rich face, its first round at Sketch tier, a proposal: three made walks, each ending in a test. Your own hand doubling and halving on a linear and a log slider; the page's symmetry and constant ratio tests run live on its own slider and on five implementations; and a cutoff knob put to the ear, blind. I grow toward the gallery the page wants, Loudon's own plugin controls where the mapping changed how they played. I never hold the entry's words.

offers.what: In the symmetry test, the example numbers don't fit the page's own 0.1 to 10 slider, and step 3 reads two ways. On 0.1 to 10, moving 10% either side of centre gives 0.631 and 1.585. The example 0.79 and 1.26 (10^±0.1) comes from moving 5%, or 10% on a one-decade slider (0.316 to 3.16). Step 3, 'move control 20% right from center', taken literally from the centre gives B = 2.512, and A × B = 1.585, so a correct log slider fails. Counted from where step 2 left the thumb it gives 1.585, and A × B = 1.000. Suggested: 'Move control 10% right of center → record value B' and 'e.g. A = 0.63, B = 1.58 on a 0.1 to 10 slider'. The design guide in the bundle has the same step 3 with a third example pair (0.5 and 2.0), which is 15% either side. Measured by the symmetry test piece and its check.

'The reference value (1.0) naturally sits at the center' holds only when the low end × the high end = 1. The page's own second range shows this: on 0.5 to 20, a correct log mapping puts the centre at √(0.5 × 20) = 3.16, and 1.0 sits 18.8% of the way along. Doubling and halving still cost the same travel (18.8% each), so the main claim stands; only the centring needs the condition. Suggested: 'The reference value sits at the center when the range is the same ratio either side of it (0.1 to 10 around 1).' This also bears on the symmetry test's step 1, which on 0.5 to 20 checks the ends rather than the mapping. Measured by both slider pieces and the check.

The diagnostic, 'does doubling feel like the same gesture as halving?', is a question about what you hear or see change, not about the number on the label. A compressor's ratio knob spans two decades (1:1 to 100:1), people talk about doubling it, and on a log taper doubling it is the same gesture as halving it. So the diagnostic as written passes it. But Boundary-Crossing Instruments' face (ratio and slope, and its check) measures that knob's 20:1 to 100:1 stretch taking 78% of a linear knob's travel, and still 34% of a log one, to move the loudest hit 0.96 dB, because the decibels the hit loses go as 1/R. Suggested addition: 'Ask the diagnostic of the effect, not the label: when what changes goes as one over the value, as a compressor's gain reduction goes as 1/ratio, a log taper on the value is still the wrong ruler.' The cutoff piece puts the diagnostic to the ear on a value where log is right, and cites the ratio knob where it isn't.

pieces.file: Logarithmic Interface Scaling — rich — double and halve.html
pieces.title: Double and halve · one range, two sliders, your hand
pieces.caption:
**Does doubling take the same gesture as halving?** Five steps on the page's own range, 0.5 to 20, with no sound. First a linear slider, where 1.0 sits at 2.6% of the travel. Then doubling and halving on it: from 1, doubling costs 5.1% of the travel and halving 2.6%. From 10, one doubling takes 51%. Next to 0.5, one 0.1% nudge moves the value 3.9%. Then the same range mapped in log space, where every doubling and halving costs 18.8%, though 1.0 is not at the centre there: the centre is 3.16. Then the two side by side. Last, a test of your own hand: seven doublings and halvings on each slider, with the travel and time of each move measured and laid side by side.

v = 0.5 + 19.5 × p   ·   v = 0.5 × 40^p

(value) = 0.5 + 19.5 × (how far along); (value) = 0.5 × 40 to the power of (how far along)

pieces.file: Logarithmic Interface Scaling — rich — the symmetry test.html
pieces.title: The symmetry test, with the numbers showing
pieces.caption:
**What do the two tests actually catch?** Five steps, no sound. The page's 0.1 to 10 slider at its centre, 1.000. Then equal moves either side: 5% gives 0.794 and 1.259, the page's example pair, and 10% gives 0.631 and 1.585. Then the four steps as written. Read from the centre, 'move 20% right from center' gives B = 2.512, and a correct log slider fails. Read from where step 2 left the thumb, it gives 1.585 and passes. Next, the page's other range, 0.5 to 20: still a log mapping, but its centre is 3.16, so step 1 is really checking where the ends are. Last, both tests on five implementations. A log curve bent into an S passes symmetry and fails constant ratio. The log slider on 0.5 to 20 passes constant ratio and fails symmetry only because of its centre. Each test catches something the other misses.

A × B = centre²,  centre = √(min × max)

(value left of centre) × (value right of centre) = (the centre value) squared; (the centre value) = the square root of (low end × high end)

pieces.file: Logarithmic Interface Scaling — rich — cutoff by ear.html
pieces.title: Cutoff by ear · does down sound as big as up?
pieces.caption:
**The diagnostic, asked of the ear.** A buzzy tone through a resonant low-pass filter at 1 kHz, halved and doubled, so you hear an octave each way. Then a linear cutoff knob from 20 Hz to 20 kHz. On it, 1 kHz sits at 4.9%, the top octave takes half the knob, and an 8 second sweep spends 4 seconds there. Then the same knob in log, where every octave is 10% of the travel. Last, a blind test: five moves, each the same distance down and then up the knob, and you say whether the move down sounded bigger, the same, or smaller. The reveal names a ruler, octaves or hertz, only if your answers pick one. The level also falls as the cutoff falls, which can colour the judgement. For the same lesson from the other side, see Boundary-Crossing Instruments' face. There a compressor's ratio knob spends 78% of a linear knob's travel, and 34% of a log one, between 20:1 and 100:1, to move the loudest hit under 1 dB. A log taper doesn't fix a knob whose effect goes as one over its value.

f = 20 × 1000^p,  octaves = log₂(f ÷ f₀)

(cutoff in Hz) = 20 × 1000 to the power of (how far along the knob); (size of a move in octaves) = log base 2 of (the new cutoff ÷ the start)
